newsitem.title: UK: Karnal Bunt in Tennessee hits US wheat prices.
newsitem.headline: Karnal Bunt in Tennessee hits US wheat prices.

text.p: News that the Karnal Bunt fungus had been found in Tennessee delivered a new hit to weakening benchmark U.S. wheat prices on Thursday.
Detection of the fungus, named for the place in India where it was found and also called Stinking Smut, often leads some nations to curb imports from affected areas.
Further news of fresh subsidised European wheat exports also undermined prices on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) and the near-month December futures fell below $3.75 per bushel.

This was down some 7-1/2 cents on the day and extended a retreat from historic highs at $7.50 back in March, before bumper harvests in several countries promised to begin replenishing depleted world grain stocks.
A spokesman for the Tennessee Department of Agriculture said the fungus was found in winter wheat grown in one Tennessee county and was suspected in six other counties as well.
The Tennessee Department of Agriculture is taking extraordinary control measures but spokesman Tom Womack said: "It would be too early to talk about a quarantine."
The European Union on Thursday granted export licences for 233,700 tonnes of free market soft wheat at a rebate up to 19.98 Ecus per tonne.

Chicago soybean futures dropped on heavier-than-expected delivery notices posted on Thursday on the November futures contract of 3.4 million bushels. Futures fell by up to eight cents with November trading just above $6.80 per bushel.
Elsewhere in commodity markets precious metals were more stable after sharp losses earlier in the week with gold ending in London at $379.75 after $380.05 on Wednesday.
Talk that European central banks may sell gold as European Union countries seek to meet the 1999 single currency criteria has been depressing sentiment, dealers said.

The world price of copper edged up and ended the afternoon session on the London Metal Exchange (LME) around $1,958 per tonne in a rebound from a Tuesday sell-off that saw it as low as $1,916. Dealers say positive supply-demand fundamentals seem to be encouraging buying of copper. But rallies are being sold in to, perhaps by banks that took on a hoard of copper built up by Yasuo Hamanaka, the disgraced Sumitomo Corp dealer.
Hamanaka built up a big long position before he was fired in June as an alleged rogue trader.
Copper prices will weaken further during the final part of this year and the trend will continue in 1997 as stocks rise, the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) said.

In its latest edition of world commodity forecasts the London-based EIU also said aluminium was undervalued, but will stay around $1,500/1,550 a tonne until early 1998 when an increase in demand will lead to some recovery in prices. Aluminium ended the London afternoon at $1,437.
Sugar weakened with the London spot December white sugar contract tumbling through major technical chart support at $310 a tonne. Selling was mostly in reaction to a bearish technical picture.
Crude oil prices were easier below $23.50 per barrel for the December contract for benchmark Brent Blend crude from the North Sea. Coffee and cocoa were just easier.
